Hal Elrod is the creator of The Miracle Morning, a bestselling book and personal development method that has helped millions improve their daily habits. Hal introduces his six-part SAVERS framework, explaining how meditation, affirmations, visualization, exercise, reading, and journaling can transform your morning in as little as six minutes. They explore how smartphones disrupt attention, why visualization works best when paired with mental rehearsal, and how these techniques can help overcome procrastination. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. She went on to run the Strategic Partnerships and Innovations team working across the ecosystem to create and nurture alliances to further the adoption of functional medicine. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. GLP-1s Are Melting Fat — But What About Your MUSCLE?

GLP-1 drugs like Wegovy and Zepbound can produce dramatic weight loss. But when someone loses 40 or 50 pounds, there's an important question most people aren't asking: How much of that weight was fat — and how much was lean mass? In this video, Peptide A to Z examines the growing concern around GLP-1 drugs and muscle loss. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? In this video, we break down how VK2735 works, GLP-1 + GIP signaling, the new maintenance data, side effects, limitations of the study, and why the next generation of obesity drugs may compete not only on how much weight people lose — but how rarely they need to take the medication. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. Peptide science without the hype. ⚠️ Educational and informational purposes only. Not medical advice. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? In this video, we break down how VK2735 works, GLP-1 + GIP signaling, the new maintenance data, side effects, limitations of the study, and why the next generation of obesity drugs may compete not only on how much weight people lose — but how rarely they need to take the medication. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. Peptide science without the hype. ⚠️ Educational and informational purposes only. Not medical advice. CJC-1295 is not FDA-approved for anti-aging, muscle building, or fat loss. #CJC1295 #Peptides #GrowthHormone #PeptideResearch #IGF1 ⚠️ DISCLAIMER This video is for educational purposes only. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? In this video, we break down how VK2735 works, GLP-1 + GIP signaling, the new maintenance data, side effects, limitations of the study, and why the next generation of obesity drugs may compete not only on how much weight people lose — but how rarely they need to take the medication. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. If you’re always feeling hungry, it may not simply be about willpower. Appetite is influenced by biological signals, including gut-to-brain communication that helps regulate fullness and energy balance. In this video, we break down how GLP-1 works in a clear and simple way, helping you better understand the science behind appetite and modern weight management research. Topics covered: • Why constant hunger happens • How GLP-1 peptides influence appetite • Gut-to-brain signaling explained simply • Why biology often matters more than willpower Learn more: https://genomaxis.com/ Genomaxis Labs focuses on research-based insights into GLP-1 peptides, metabolism, and modern approaches to weight management. Disclaimer: This content is for informational and educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice.

We converted raw polypropylene pellets into finished pallets of masks. I had a background in software from my YC W10 company, so we took a software approach to building our factory. We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. We built an efficient manufacturing operation and grew the business to 50 million dollars in revenue. Then people actually stopped caring about masks. Fair enough. Around the same time, I decided to try and lose the weight I had gained while building the factory. I ate nothing but chicken for six months. While this diet got some results, I plateaued. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. Peptide science without the hype. ⚠️ Educational and informational purposes only. Not medical advice. CJC-1295 is not FDA-approved for anti-aging, muscle building, or fat loss. #CJC1295 #Peptides #GrowthHormone #PeptideResearch #IGF1 ⚠️ DISCLAIMER This video is for educational purposes only. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? In this video, we break down how VK2735 works, GLP-1 + GIP signaling, the new maintenance data, side effects, limitations of the study, and why the next generation of obesity drugs may compete not only on how much weight people lose — but how rarely they need to take the medication. Launch HN: RonanRX (YC S26) – Personalized Peptides and GLP-1s

Hi HN, I’m Lloyd, one of two founders of RonanRx ( https://ronanrx.com/ ). We are building a vertically integrated pharmaceutical company with software for prescribing, telehealth, compounding, manufacturing, and delivery. We are starting with GLP-1s and peptides. The path to RonanRx is fairly unconventional. During the pandemic, I built one of the largest mask manufacturing factories in the US. We could make a million masks in a day. We converted raw polypropylene pellets into finished pallets of masks. I had a background in software from my YC W10 company, so we took a software approach to building our factory. We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. We built an efficient manufacturing operation and grew the business to 50 million dollars in revenue. Then people actually stopped caring about masks. Fair enough. Around the same time, I decided to try and lose the weight I had gained while building the factory. I ate nothing but chicken for six months. While this diet got some results, I plateaued. My doctor suggested tirzepatide, a GLP-1 medication. For me, losing weight was only the beginning. "Food noise" was gone. I showed less interest in other compulsive behavior. I stopped scrolling Instagram and quit biting my nails. But that was just the beginning. I was born with a congenital heart defect called aortic stenosis. My whole life doctors told me I'd need open heart surgery in my…

CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?

Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. Peptide science without the hype. ⚠️ Educational and informational purposes only. Not medical advice. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? payload.summary: What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. GLP-1s Are Melting Fat — But What About Your MUSCLE?

GLP-1 drugs like Wegovy and Zepbound can produce dramatic weight loss. But when someone loses 40 or 50 pounds, there's an important question most people aren't asking: How much of that weight was fat — and how much was lean mass? Your Relationship Shouldn't Be A Drag

Ep. 1012: Join us as we sit down with Margarita Nazarenko – globally recognised voice in feminine psychology, confidence, and identity. Margarita has built a large audience around her unfiltered takes on womanhood, dating, personal growth, and building a life on your own terms. In this episode, Margarita breaks down why seeking validation from a partner can quietly change the way you show up in a relationship — and how learning to validate yourself can shift everything. Margarita gets candid about anxious attachment, people-pleasing, relationship adrenaline, and the childhood patterns that can influence who we become in love. She shares the counterintuitive ways to handle conflict, boundaries, communication, and disrespect without chasing, or giving away your power. She also reveals the mindset shift that changed the way she approached relationships and ultimately helped her create the life and marriage she wanted.

GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. They discuss preparing your body for pregnancy, postpartum wellness, the power of Pilates, and the importance of protecting your time, privacy, and energy in an always-on world. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? In this video, we break down how VK2735 works, GLP-1 + GIP signaling, the new maintenance data, side effects, limitations of the study, and why the next generation of obesity drugs may compete not only on how much weight people lose — but how rarely they need to take the medication. Its active ingredient, orforglipron, is a non-peptide small molecule designed to activate the GLP-1 receptor. And it's not the only option. Wegovy is now available as an oral semaglutide tablet, giving patients another alternative to weekly GLP-1 injections. One of the most interesting developments is the science itself. Oral Wegovy contains the peptide semaglutide and uses a formulation designed to help it be absorbed orally. Foundayo takes a completely different approach: orforglipron is a small molecule rather than a peptide, but it targets the same GLP-1 receptor. BPC-157 Is EXPLODING — New Data Shows a 33X Surge

BPC-157 use appears to be exploding. New 2026 research found a 33-fold increase in newly documented BPC-157 users, rising from just 4 in the first quarter of 2020 to 134 in the first quarter of 2026 within a large medical-record network. But the most surprising number may be 79%. Among BPC-157 users whose medical records contained a clear outcome, about 79% had improvement documented. Does that mean BPC-157 actually works? Not so fast. In this video, Peptide A to Z breaks down the new BPC-157 research, including: • Where the 33X increase actually comes from • Why documented BPC-157 use is rising • What people are using BPC-157 for • The truth behind the reported 79% improvement rate • Why most improvements were patient-reported • BPC-157 and TB-500 — the “Wolverine Stack” • What the FDA says about BPC-157 • Why BPC-157 is still not FDA approved • What human evidence we actually have • What researchers still need to prove The new study examined clinical records from a network covering 15.2 million patients and identified 1,039 confirmed BPC-157 users. It's one of the most interesting looks yet at how this controversial peptide is being used in the real world. But there's an important distinction between popularity and proof. The study was observational, had no placebo group, did not use a standardized BPC-157 dose or treatment period, and many patients were using other therapies at the same time. The research was also released as a preprint and has not yet completed peer…

GLP-1s Are Melting Fat — But What About Your MUSCLE?

GLP-1 drugs like Wegovy and Zepbound can produce dramatic weight loss. But when someone loses 40 or 50 pounds, there's an important question most people aren't asking: How much of that weight was fat — and how much was lean mass? In this video, Peptide A to Z examines the growing concern around GLP-1 drugs and muscle loss. Research shows that people taking GLP-1 medications can lose measurable amounts of lean body mass along with fat. So yes, lean mass can decrease. But substantially more fat was lost, meaning overall body composition improved. Now researchers want to know whether they can do even better. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? In this video, we break down how VK2735 works, GLP-1 + GIP signaling, the new maintenance data, side effects, limitations of the study, and why the next generation of obesity drugs may compete not only on how much weight people lose — but how rarely they need to take the medication. One of the most interesting developments is the science itself. Oral Wegovy contains the peptide semaglutide and uses a formulation designed to help it be absorbed orally. Foundayo takes a completely different approach: orforglipron is a small molecule rather than a peptide, but it targets the same GLP-1 receptor. BPC-157 Is EXPLODING — New Data Shows a 33X Surge

BPC-157 use appears to be exploding. New 2026 research found a 33-fold increase in newly documented BPC-157 users, rising from just 4 in the first quarter of 2020 to 134 in the first quarter of 2026 within a large medical-record network. But the most surprising number may be 79%. Among BPC-157 users whose medical records contained a clear outcome, about 79% had improvement documented. Does that mean BPC-157 actually works? Not so fast. It's one of the most interesting looks yet at how this controversial peptide is being used in the real world. But there's an important distinction between popularity and proof. Launch HN: RonanRX (YC S26) – Personalized Peptides and GLP-1s

Hi HN, I’m Lloyd, one of two founders of RonanRx ( https://ronanrx.com/ ). We are building a vertically integrated pharmaceutical company with software for prescribing, telehealth, compounding, manufacturing, and delivery. We are starting with GLP-1s and peptides. The path to RonanRx is fairly unconventional. During the pandemic, I built one of the largest mask manufacturing factories in the US. We could make a million masks in a day. We converted raw polypropylene pellets into finished pallets of masks. I had a background in software from my YC W10 company, so we took a software approach to building our factory. We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. We built an efficient manufacturing operation and grew the business to 50 million dollars in revenue. Then people actually stopped caring about masks. Fair enough. Around the same time, I decided to try and lose the weight I had gained while building the factory. I ate nothing but chicken for six months. While this diet got some results, I plateaued. My doctor suggested tirzepatide, a GLP-1 medication. For me, losing weight was only the beginning. "Food noise" was gone. I showed less interest in other compulsive behavior. I stopped scrolling Instagram and quit biting my nails. But that was just the beginning. I was born with a congenital heart defect called aortic stenosis. My whole life doctors told me I'd need open heart surgery in my…

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? Hi HN, I’m Lloyd, one of two founders of RonanRx ( https://ronanrx.com/ ). We are building a vertically integrated pharmaceutical company with software for prescribing, telehealth, compounding, manufacturing, and delivery. We are starting with GLP-1s and peptides. The path to RonanRx is fairly unconventional. During the pandemic, I built one of the largest mask manufacturing factories in the US. We could make a million masks in a day. We converted raw polypropylene pellets into finished pallets of masks. I had a background in software from my YC W10 company, so we took a software approach to building our factory. We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. We built an efficient manufacturing operation and grew the business to 50 million dollars in revenue. Then people actually stopped caring about masks. Fair enough. Around the same time, I decided to try and lose the weight I had gained while building the factory. I ate nothing but chicken for six months. While this diet got some results, I plateaued. My doctor suggested tirzepatide, a GLP-1 medication. For me, losing weight was only the beginning. "Food noise" was gone. I showed less interest in other compulsive behavior. I stopped scrolling Instagram and quit biting my nails. But that was just the beginning. I was born with a congenital heart defect called aortic stenosis. My whole life doctors told me I'd need open heart surgery in my…

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. Orexin Explained: The Peptide That Keeps Your Brain Awake

What if one tiny peptide system in your brain helps determine whether you stay awake or fall asleep? In this episode of Peptide A to Z, we break down orexin, a naturally occurring peptide system that plays a major role in wakefulness, alertness, sleep, and narcolepsy. People with narcolepsy type 1 lose most of the brain cells that produce orexin. Without enough orexin signaling, the brain can struggle to maintain the normal boundary between being awake and asleep—leading to severe daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and other symptoms. But in 2026, the orexin story reached a major milestone. We explore how researchers developed a new approach that targets the orexin 2 receptor, why this is fundamentally different from simply using a stimulant, and how the same peptide system can actually be targeted in the opposite direction to help treat insomnia. In this video: • What orexin A and orexin B are • How orexin helps keep the brain awake • The connection between orexin and narcolepsy type 1 • What cataplexy is • The 2026 breakthrough in orexin-targeted treatment • Why blocking orexin can help people sleep • Orexin's potential roles in appetite, motivation, reward, stress, and metabolism • Why this peptide system could become increasingly important in medicine One peptide system. Launch HN: RonanRX (YC S26) – Personalized Peptides and GLP-1s

Hi HN, I’m Lloyd, one of two founders of RonanRx ( https://ronanrx.com/ ). We are building a vertically integrated pharmaceutical company with software for prescribing, telehealth, compounding, manufacturing, and delivery. We are starting with GLP-1s and peptides. The path to RonanRx is fairly unconventional. During the pandemic, I built one of the largest mask manufacturing factories in the US. We could make a million masks in a day. We converted raw polypropylene pellets into finished pallets of masks. I had a background in software from my YC W10 company, so we took a software approach to building our factory. We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? In this video, we break down how VK2735 works, GLP-1 + GIP signaling, the new maintenance data, side effects, limitations of the study, and why the next generation of obesity drugs may compete not only on how much weight people lose — but how rarely they need to take the medication. Orexin Explained: The Peptide That Keeps Your Brain Awake

What if one tiny peptide system in your brain helps determine whether you stay awake or fall asleep? In this episode of Peptide A to Z, we break down orexin, a naturally occurring peptide system that plays a major role in wakefulness, alertness, sleep, and narcolepsy. People with narcolepsy type 1 lose most of the brain cells that produce orexin. Without enough orexin signaling, the brain can struggle to maintain the normal boundary between being awake and asleep—leading to severe daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and other symptoms. But in 2026, the orexin story reached a major milestone. We explore how researchers developed a new approach that targets the orexin 2 receptor, why this is fundamentally different from simply using a stimulant, and how the same peptide system can actually be targeted in the opposite direction to help treat insomnia. In this video: • What orexin A and orexin B are • How orexin helps keep the brain awake • The connection between orexin and narcolepsy type 1 • What cataplexy is • The 2026 breakthrough in orexin-targeted treatment • Why blocking orexin can help people sleep • Orexin's potential roles in appetite, motivation, reward, stress, and metabolism • Why this peptide system could become increasingly important in medicine One peptide system. GLP-1 Once a Month?! New VK2735 Results Could Change Weight Loss

What if you didn't have to take a GLP-1 every week — but only once a month? New clinical trial results for VK2735, an experimental GLP-1/GIP drug from Viking Therapeutics, suggest that less-frequent dosing could eventually play a role in maintaining weight loss. In the study, participants first received weekly VK2735 and lost approximately 16% to 19% of their body weight after 21 weeks. Researchers then tested less-frequent maintenance dosing. The results were fascinating: 💉 Every-other-week dosing maintained up to 97% of previous weight loss 📅 Once-monthly dosing maintained up to 90% ⚖️ Participants switched to placebo maintained about 61% 📉 A small weekly-treatment group reached an average 21.7% weight loss after 33 weeks But there's an important distinction: this does not mean people started with a once-a-month injection and lost 20% of their body weight. Participants first lost weight using weekly VK2735. Researchers then tested whether less-frequent dosing could help maintain those results. That raises a much bigger question for the future of GLP-1 treatment: Could people eventually lose weight with weekly injections, then transition to one injection a month for maintenance? In this video, we break down how VK2735 works, GLP-1 + GIP signaling, the new maintenance data, side effects, limitations of the study, and why the next generation of obesity drugs may compete not only on how much weight people lose — but how rarely they need to take the medication. Orexin Explained: The Peptide That Keeps Your Brain Awake

What if one tiny peptide system in your brain helps determine whether you stay awake or fall asleep? In this episode of Peptide A to Z, we break down orexin, a naturally occurring peptide system that plays a major role in wakefulness, alertness, sleep, and narcolepsy. People with narcolepsy type 1 lose most of the brain cells that produce orexin. Without enough orexin signaling, the brain can struggle to maintain the normal boundary between being awake and asleep—leading to severe daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and other symptoms. But in 2026, the orexin story reached a major milestone. We explore how researchers developed a new approach that targets the orexin 2 receptor, why this is fundamentally different from simply using a stimulant, and how the same peptide system can actually be targeted in the opposite direction to help treat insomnia. Orexin Explained: The Peptide That Keeps Your Brain Awake

What if one tiny peptide system in your brain helps determine whether you stay awake or fall asleep? In this episode of Peptide A to Z, we break down orexin, a naturally occurring peptide system that plays a major role in wakefulness, alertness, sleep, and narcolepsy. People with narcolepsy type 1 lose most of the brain cells that produce orexin. Without enough orexin signaling, the brain can struggle to maintain the normal boundary between being awake and asleep—leading to severe daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and other symptoms. But in 2026, the orexin story reached a major milestone. We explore how researchers developed a new approach that targets the orexin 2 receptor, why this is fundamentally different from simply using a stimulant, and how the same peptide system can actually be targeted in the opposite direction to help treat insomnia. In this video: • What orexin A and orexin B are • How orexin helps keep the brain awake • The connection between orexin and narcolepsy type 1 • What cataplexy is • The 2026 breakthrough in orexin-targeted treatment • Why blocking orexin can help people sleep • Orexin's potential roles in appetite, motivation, reward, stress, and metabolism • Why this peptide system could become increasingly important in medicine One peptide system. Turn it down to help people sleep. Turn it up to help people stay awake. Subscribe to Peptide A to Z for straightforward breakdowns of peptide research, clinical studies, and emerging…

embedding_text:
The Peptide That Actually Builds Bone? 65% Lower Fracture Risk

Can a peptide actually BUILD new bone? Forteo, also known as teriparatide, is an FDA-approved peptide medicine with something most peptides discussed online don't have: large human trials and evidence showing fewer fractures. In this video, we break down how Forteo works, why it can stimulate new bone formation, and the major human trial where the standard dose was associated with about a 65% lower relative risk of new spinal fractures compared with placebo. We also look at one of the most fascinating parts of its history: early animal studies raised concerns about bone tumors, Forteo originally carried an FDA boxed warning, and years of human safety evidence eventually led the FDA to remove that boxed warning. This is a perfect example of why the question isn't simply “Do peptides work?” The better question is: Which peptide, for what purpose, and where is the human evidence? 📘 FREE Peptide Guide: PeptideAtoZ.com/free-guide 💬 Join the Peptide A to Z Community: PeptideAtoZ.com/community 🔬 Peptide A to Z Research. We are building a vertically integrated pharmaceutical company with software for prescribing, telehealth, compounding, manufacturing, and delivery. We are starting with GLP-1s and peptides. The path to RonanRx is fairly unconventional. During the pandemic, I built one of the largest mask manufacturing factories in the US. We could make a million masks in a day. We converted raw polypropylene pellets into finished pallets of masks. I had a background in software from my YC W10 company, so we took a software approach to building our factory. We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. We built an efficient manufacturing operation and grew the business to 50 million dollars in revenue. Then people actually stopped caring about masks. Fair enough. Around the same time, I decided to try and lose the weight I had gained while building the factory. I ate nothing but chicken for six months. While this diet got some results, I plateaued. My doctor suggested tirzepatide, a GLP-1 medication. For me, losing weight was only the beginning. "Food noise" was gone. I showed less interest in other compulsive behavior. I stopped scrolling Instagram and quit biting my nails. But that was just the beginning. I was born with a congenital heart defect called aortic stenosis. Orexin Explained: The Peptide That Keeps Your Brain Awake

What if one tiny peptide system in your brain helps determine whether you stay awake or fall asleep? In this episode of Peptide A to Z, we break down orexin, a naturally occurring peptide system that plays a major role in wakefulness, alertness, sleep, and narcolepsy. People with narcolepsy type 1 lose most of the brain cells that produce orexin. Without enough orexin signaling, the brain can struggle to maintain the normal boundary between being awake and asleep—leading to severe daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and other symptoms. But in 2026, the orexin story reached a major milestone. We explore how researchers developed a new approach that targets the orexin 2 receptor, why this is fundamentally different from simply using a stimulant, and how the same peptide system can actually be targeted in the opposite direction to help treat insomnia. The Peptide That Actually Builds Bone? 65% Lower Fracture Risk

Can a peptide actually BUILD new bone? Forteo, also known as teriparatide, is an FDA-approved peptide medicine with something most peptides discussed online don't have: large human trials and evidence showing fewer fractures. In this video, we break down how Forteo works, why it can stimulate new bone formation, and the major human trial where the standard dose was associated with about a 65% lower relative risk of new spinal fractures compared with placebo. We also look at one of the most fascinating parts of its history: early animal studies raised concerns about bone tumors, Forteo originally carried an FDA boxed warning, and years of human safety evidence eventually led the FDA to remove that boxed warning. It's one of the most interesting looks yet at how this controversial peptide is being used in the real world. But there's an important distinction between popularity and proof. The study was observational, had no placebo group, did not use a standardized BPC-157 dose or treatment period, and many patients were using other therapies at the same time. Orexin Explained: The Peptide That Keeps Your Brain Awake

What if one tiny peptide system in your brain helps determine whether you stay awake or fall asleep? In this episode of Peptide A to Z, we break down orexin, a naturally occurring peptide system that plays a major role in wakefulness, alertness, sleep, and narcolepsy. People with narcolepsy type 1 lose most of the brain cells that produce orexin. Without enough orexin signaling, the brain can struggle to maintain the normal boundary between being awake and asleep—leading to severe daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and other symptoms. But in 2026, the orexin story reached a major milestone. We explore how researchers developed a new approach that targets the orexin 2 receptor, why this is fundamentally different from simply using a stimulant, and how the same peptide system can actually be targeted in the opposite direction to help treat insomnia. In this video: • What orexin A and orexin B are • How orexin helps keep the brain awake • The connection between orexin and narcolepsy type 1 • What cataplexy is • The 2026 breakthrough in orexin-targeted treatment • Why blocking orexin can help people sleep • Orexin's potential roles in appetite, motivation, reward, stress, and metabolism • Why this peptide system could become increasingly important in medicine One peptide system. Turn it down to help people sleep. Turn it up to help people stay awake. Subscribe to Peptide A to Z for straightforward breakdowns of peptide research, clinical studies, and emerging…

The Peptide That Actually Builds Bone? 65% Lower Fracture Risk

Can a peptide actually BUILD new bone? Forteo, also known as teriparatide, is an FDA-approved peptide medicine with something most peptides discussed online don't have: large human trials and evidence showing fewer fractures. In this video, we break down how Forteo works, why it can stimulate new bone formation, and the major human trial where the standard dose was associated with about a 65% lower relative risk of new spinal fractures compared with placebo. We also look at one of the most fascinating parts of its history: early animal studies raised concerns about bone tumors, Forteo originally carried an FDA boxed warning, and years of human safety evidence eventually led the FDA to remove that boxed warning. The path to RonanRx is fairly unconventional. During the pandemic, I built one of the largest mask manufacturing factories in the US. We could make a million masks in a day. We converted raw polypropylene pellets into finished pallets of masks. I had a background in software from my YC W10 company, so we took a software approach to building our factory. We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. We built an efficient manufacturing operation and grew the business to 50 million dollars in revenue. Then people actually stopped caring about masks. Fair enough. Around the same time, I decided to try and lose the weight I had gained while building the factory. I ate nothing but chicken for six months. While this diet got some results, I plateaued. Orexin Explained: The Peptide That Keeps Your Brain Awake

What if one tiny peptide system in your brain helps determine whether you stay awake or fall asleep? In this episode of Peptide A to Z, we break down orexin, a naturally occurring peptide system that plays a major role in wakefulness, alertness, sleep, and narcolepsy. People with narcolepsy type 1 lose most of the brain cells that produce orexin. Without enough orexin signaling, the brain can struggle to maintain the normal boundary between being awake and asleep—leading to severe daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and other symptoms. But in 2026, the orexin story reached a major milestone. We explore how researchers developed a new approach that targets the orexin 2 receptor, why this is fundamentally different from simply using a stimulant, and how the same peptide system can actually be targeted in the opposite direction to help treat insomnia. The Peptide That Actually Builds Bone? 65% Lower Fracture Risk

Can a peptide actually BUILD new bone? Forteo, also known as teriparatide, is an FDA-approved peptide medicine with something most peptides discussed online don't have: large human trials and evidence showing fewer fractures. In this video, we break down how Forteo works, why it can stimulate new bone formation, and the major human trial where the standard dose was associated with about a 65% lower relative risk of new spinal fractures compared with placebo. We also look at one of the most fascinating parts of its history: early animal studies raised concerns about bone tumors, Forteo originally carried an FDA boxed warning, and years of human safety evidence eventually led the FDA to remove that boxed warning. Orexin Explained: The Peptide That Keeps Your Brain Awake

What if one tiny peptide system in your brain helps determine whether you stay awake or fall asleep? In this episode of Peptide A to Z, we break down orexin, a naturally occurring peptide system that plays a major role in wakefulness, alertness, sleep, and narcolepsy. People with narcolepsy type 1 lose most of the brain cells that produce orexin. Without enough orexin signaling, the brain can struggle to maintain the normal boundary between being awake and asleep—leading to severe daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and other symptoms. But in 2026, the orexin story reached a major milestone. We explore how researchers developed a new approach that targets the orexin 2 receptor, why this is fundamentally different from simply using a stimulant, and how the same peptide system can actually be targeted in the opposite direction to help treat insomnia. The Peptide That Actually Builds Bone? 65% Lower Fracture Risk

Can a peptide actually BUILD new bone? Forteo, also known as teriparatide, is an FDA-approved peptide medicine with something most peptides discussed online don't have: large human trials and evidence showing fewer fractures. In this video, we break down how Forteo works, why it can stimulate new bone formation, and the major human trial where the standard dose was associated with about a 65% lower relative risk of new spinal fractures compared with placebo. We also look at one of the most fascinating parts of its history: early animal studies raised concerns about bone tumors, Forteo originally carried an FDA boxed warning, and years of human safety evidence eventually led the FDA to remove that boxed warning. YOUNGER: The Seat of the Soul with Gary Zukav

“The choice that frees or imprisons us is the choice of love or fear. Love liberates. Fear imprisons “. -- Gary Zukav, Spiritual Teacher and New York Times Bestselling Author. Gary Zukav (born October 17, 1942) is an American spiritual teacher, and the author of four consecutive New York Times Best Sellers. Beginning in 1998, he appeared more than 30 times on The Oprah Winfrey Show to discuss transformation in human consciousness which were concepts he presented in his book, The Seat of the Soul. Gary’s first book, The Dancing Wu Li Masters (1979), won a U.S. National Book Award. It is an overview of the New Physics, and became the winner of The American Book Award for Science. Gary’s book The Seat of the Soul, was celebrated as a #1 New York Times Bestseller for three consecutive years in a row. His book, Soul Stories, was also a New York Times bestselling book; and many other books he has written that followed. Gary’s books have sold millions of copies and are published in twenty-four languages. He is a graduate of Harvard University and a former U.S. Army Special Forces (Green Beret) officer with Vietnam service. Gary lives in Oregon. Linda Francis was his spiritual partner for decades. She passed on in 2022, and Gary has said, “She (Linda) was a model to me and many others.” Dr. Robyn Benson's next YOUNGER podcast episode is an interview with "The Seat of the Soul" New York Times Bestselling Author, Gary Zukav. Watch, listen and learn from this powerful, timely video…

Neuroscientist: Alzheimer's Starts In Your Nose (Here’s the Fix)

**Visit https://memoryair.com/ and use code DAVE15 for 15% off. ** Dr. Michael Leon on Smell Training, Memory, Sleep, Alzheimer’s Risk, and Brain Longevity Your sense of smell may reveal more about your brain health than you realize, and stimulating it while you sleep may improve memory, sleep quality, and cognitive function. Host Dave Asprey sits down with Dr. Michael Leon, Professor Emeritus of Neurobiology and Behavior at UC Irvine and one of the world’s most cited scientists, to explore why smell may be one of the most overlooked tools for brain health and longevity. Dr. Leon explains why the olfactory system has unusually direct access to the brain’s memory and emotional centers, why smell often declines alongside memory after age 60, and why reduced olfactory function has been associated with Alzheimer’s disease, cognitive decline, depression, and increased all-cause mortality. They also discuss how COVID, chronic congestion, pollution, stress, and aging can impair smell without people realizing it. The conversation dives into olfactory enrichment, including research showing major improvements in memory when older adults were exposed to multiple scents during sleep. Dr. Leon explains why novelty matters, how nighttime scent exposure may increase deep sleep and reduce nightmares, and why olfactory stimulation is being studied in dementia, PTSD, depression, and autism. Dave also explores connections between smell, GLP-1 drugs, exercise, rapamycin, spermidine, oxytocin…

But the most surprising number may be 79%. Among BPC-157 users whose medical records contained a clear outcome, about 79% had improvement documented. Does that mean BPC-157 actually works? Orexin Explained: The Peptide That Keeps Your Brain Awake

What if one tiny peptide system in your brain helps determine whether you stay awake or fall asleep? In this episode of Peptide A to Z, we break down orexin, a naturally occurring peptide system that plays a major role in wakefulness, alertness, sleep, and narcolepsy. People with narcolepsy type 1 lose most of the brain cells that produce orexin. Without enough orexin signaling, the brain can struggle to maintain the normal boundary between being awake and asleep—leading to severe daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and other symptoms. But in 2026, the orexin story reached a major milestone. We explore how researchers developed a new approach that targets the orexin 2 receptor, why this is fundamentally different from simply using a stimulant, and how the same peptide system can actually be targeted in the opposite direction to help treat insomnia. In this video: • What orexin A and orexin B are • How orexin helps keep the brain awake • The connection between orexin and narcolepsy type 1 • What cataplexy is • The 2026 breakthrough in orexin-targeted treatment • Why blocking orexin can help people sleep • Orexin's potential roles in appetite, motivation, reward, stress, and metabolism • Why this peptide system could become increasingly important in medicine One peptide system. Turn it down to help people sleep. Turn it up to help people stay awake. Subscribe to Peptide A to Z for straightforward breakdowns of peptide research, clinical studies, and emerging…

The Peptide That Actually Builds Bone? 65% Lower Fracture Risk

Can a peptide actually BUILD new bone? Forteo, also known as teriparatide, is an FDA-approved peptide medicine with something most peptides discussed online don't have: large human trials and evidence showing fewer fractures. In this video, we break down how Forteo works, why it can stimulate new bone formation, and the major human trial where the standard dose was associated with about a 65% lower relative risk of new spinal fractures compared with placebo. We also look at one of the most fascinating parts of its history: early animal studies raised concerns about bone tumors, Forteo originally carried an FDA boxed warning, and years of human safety evidence eventually led the FDA to remove that boxed warning.
